Introduction to Cryptography

Cryptography is the science of securing information so that only intended recipients can read, verify, or act on it. It underpins every secure system — from HTTPS to messaging apps to digital currencies.

🔑 Core Definition
Cryptography provides security assurances — mathematical guarantees about what an adversary can and cannot do, even when they can observe all traffic.

The Four Security Assurances

  • Confidentiality — only the intended recipient can read the message
  • Integrity — the message has not been altered in transit
  • Authentication — the message genuinely comes from the claimed sender
  • Non-repudiation — the sender cannot later deny having sent it

What Is a Cryptographic Key?

A key is a piece of secret data that parameterises a cryptographic algorithm. The same algorithm with different keys produces completely different outputs. Modern security relies on key secrecy, not algorithm secrecy (Kerckhoffs's principle).

The OW-PASS Security Model

The naive OW-PASS (One-Way Password) model defines a minimal security goal: given a ciphertext, an attacker should not be able to recover the plaintext. This is the weakest meaningful notion of security — later modules introduce stronger models.

🔐 Back to the CipherPulse
That cryptogram at the top? It's a Caesar cipher — shift every letter back by 3 and you get: "THE CAT SAT ON THE MAT". It fails even OW-PASS because the statistical structure of English survives encryption entirely.

Classical Ciphers — Why They Fail

Before modern cryptography, ciphers relied on simple transformations that preserved the statistical structure of plaintext. Understanding their failures builds the intuition for every design decision in modern algorithms.

The Caesar Cipher

Julius Caesar encrypted messages by shifting every letter by a fixed number (e.g. shift 3: A→D, B→E, Z→C). With only 25 possible shifts, an attacker can try all of them in seconds — this is a brute-force attack.

// Caesar cipher: shift 3 Plaintext: A T T A C K A T D A W N Ciphertext: D W W D F N D W G D Z Q

The Vigenère Cipher

The Vigenère cipher uses a repeating keyword — each keyword letter defines a different Caesar shift. With key "KEY": positions cycle K=+10, E=+4, Y=+24. Considered "unbreakable" for 300 years until Kasiski (1863) found the key length by locating repeated ciphertext segments, then reduced it to independent Caesar columns broken by frequency analysis.

// Vigenère: key = "KEY", plaintext = "ATTACK" Plaintext: A T T A C K Key: K E Y K E Y // repeating Shifts: +10 +4 +24 +10 +4 +24 Ciphertext: K X R K G I

Substitution Ciphers & Frequency Analysis

A general substitution cipher maps each letter to a fixed substitute — key space 26! ≈ 4×10²⁶, far too large to brute-force. Yet they collapse under frequency analysis: in English, 'E' appears ~13% of the time. In a substitution cipher, the most frequent ciphertext letter almost certainly represents 'E'. Al-Kindi described this attack in 850 AD.

📌 Why Classical Ciphers Fail — The Core Insight
Every classical cipher preserves the statistical structure of the plaintext — letter frequencies, digrams, and word patterns survive encryption. Modern ciphers destroy all statistical structure through confusion (ciphertext statistically independent of key) and diffusion (each plaintext bit spreads across the whole ciphertext). This is precisely what the modules on symmetric cryptography, stream ciphers, and block ciphers build up to.

Module 1 — Extended Practice
This module is the hands-on companion to Module 0. You already know why classical ciphers fail — now apply that knowledge: break ciphers, run frequency analysis, and connect classical failures directly to the security goals of modern cryptography.

From Classical Failures to Modern Goals

Module 0 introduced the four security assurances and the OW-PASS model. Classical ciphers fail every one of these goals because they leak statistical information. This module traces exactly which property each cipher violates, and why it matters.

Kerckhoffs's Principle — Revisited

Classical ciphers often relied on keeping the algorithm secret (security through obscurity). Kerckhoffs's principle (1883) overturned this: a cipher must be secure even if everything except the key is public knowledge. This is the foundation of all modern algorithm design — AES, RSA, and ECDSA are all fully public.

// Security-through-obscurity vs Kerckhoffs Classical approach: "Don't tell anyone the algorithm" Problem: algorithms leak, get reverse-engineered, are shared Modern approach: "Algorithm is public; only the key is secret" Benefit: public scrutiny finds weaknesses before attackers do

The One-Time Pad — Perfect Secrecy, Impractical Key

Vernam's one-time pad (1917) XORs each plaintext bit with a truly random key bit of equal length, used exactly once. Shannon (1949) proved it achieves perfect secrecy — the ciphertext reveals zero information about the plaintext. But it requires a new random key as long as every message, which is infeasible in practice. All stream ciphers are attempts to approximate this ideal with a short key and a pseudo-random keystream.

📌 Classical → Modern Security Properties
Caesar cipher — fails OW-PASS: 25 keys, trivial brute-force
Substitution cipher — fails OW-PASS: frequency analysis despite huge key space
Vigenère cipher — fails IND-CPA: Kasiski + frequency analysis after key-length recovery
One-time pad — achieves perfect secrecy but requires key as long as message
Lesson: security must be provable, not just intuitively plausible

Symmetric Cryptography I

Symmetric cryptography uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt. This module covers the theoretical foundations — from the only provably secure cipher to the building blocks of modern stream ciphers.

The One-Time Pad (OTP)

The OTP XORs a plaintext with a truly random key of equal length. It is the only provably secure encryption scheme (Shannon, 1949). Its fatal weakness: the key must be as long as the message and never reused.

// One-Time Pad: XOR each bit of message with key Plaintext: 1 0 1 1 0 Key: 0 1 1 0 1 Ciphertext: 1 1 0 1 1 // XOR result Decrypt: 1 1 0 1 1 XOR 0 1 1 0 1 = 1 0 1 1 0 // original

The Two-Time Pad Attack

If the same OTP key is reused for two different messages — C₁ = P₁ ⊕ K and C₂ = P₂ ⊕ K — then C₁ ⊕ C₂ = P₁ ⊕ P₂. The key cancels out entirely, and the attacker has the XOR of two plaintexts, which leaks substantial information via cribs and language statistics. The Lorenz cipher was broken this way in WWII.

Stream Ciphers

A stream cipher approximates the OTP by using a short key and a Pseudo-Random Generator (PRG) to expand it into a long keystream. The keystream XORs with the plaintext — computationally indistinguishable from a true OTP if the PRG is secure.

🔑 PRG, PRF, and PRP
PRG (Pseudo-Random Generator) — stretches a short seed into a long pseudo-random bitstring
PRF (Pseudo-Random Function) — a keyed function indistinguishable from a truly random function
PRP (Pseudo-Random Permutation) — a PRF that is also bijective (invertible); block ciphers implement PRPs

Security of each: a distinguisher (efficient algorithm trying to tell the output from true randomness) should succeed with probability at most negligibly above ½.

Semantic Security

A cipher is semantically secure if encrypting two messages of the attacker's choice produces indistinguishable ciphertexts. This is the computational analogue of Shannon's perfect secrecy — achievable with short keys using a secure PRG.

Symmetric Cryptography II — Block Ciphers & AES

Block ciphers process fixed-size blocks of data and are the workhorses of symmetric cryptography. This module covers their internal design, how they are chained into modes of operation, and the formal security goal of IND-CPA.

DES vs AES

  • DES (1977) — 56-bit key, 64-bit block, 16 Feistel rounds. Broken by brute force in 22 hours in 1999. Triple-DES (3DES) patched it but is slow; now deprecated.
  • AES (Rijndael, NIST 2001) — 128/192/256-bit key, 128-bit block, 10/12/14 rounds of SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, and AddRoundKey. No practical attack known after 25+ years.

Inside AES — Four Operations per Round

// AES round (simplified) — applied 10 times for AES-128 1. SubBytes — substitute each byte via S-box (non-linear confusion) 2. ShiftRows — cyclically shift each row of the 4×4 state (diffusion) 3. MixColumns — multiply each column by a matrix over GF(2⁸) (diffusion) 4. AddRoundKey — XOR state with round key derived from master key

Modes of Operation

🔑 Four Key Modes
ECB — encrypts each block independently. Identical plaintext blocks → identical ciphertext blocks. Completely insecure for any multi-block message (reveals structure).

CBC — XORs each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encrypting. Requires a random IV. Sequential only; padding oracle attacks are a risk if not authenticated.

CTR — encrypts a counter + nonce, then XORs with plaintext. Fully parallelisable. Acts like a stream cipher. Requires a unique nonce per message — nonce reuse is catastrophic.

GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) — CTR mode + GHASH authentication. Provides both confidentiality and integrity in one pass. The modern standard (AES-256-GCM in TLS 1.3).

IND-CPA Security

Indistinguishability under Chosen Plaintext Attack (IND-CPA): an adversary who may choose any plaintexts to encrypt cannot distinguish between encryptions of two messages of their choice. ECB fails immediately — the same plaintext always gives the same ciphertext. CBC and CTR achieve IND-CPA only when IVs/nonces are freshly random for every encryption.

The ECB Penguin — Why Modes Matter Visually

The "ECB penguin" is a famous demonstration: a bitmap image of a penguin encrypted with AES-ECB is still recognisable as a penguin, because identical 16-byte pixel blocks map to identical ciphertext blocks. The same image encrypted with AES-CBC looks like random noise.

Hash Functions

A cryptographic hash function maps an input of arbitrary length to a fixed-length digest. It is a one-way function — easy to compute but infeasible to reverse — and forms the foundation of digital signatures, MACs, integrity verification, and key derivation.

Connecting Hash Functions to Block Ciphers and PRFs

Lecture 4 opens by revisiting the avalanche effect introduced for block ciphers in Week 3: a small change to the input produces a large, unpredictable change to the output. For AES, a 1-bit plaintext change flips ~50% of the ciphertext bits. Hash functions require the same property — and they achieve it for the same reason: confusion (non-linear substitution) and diffusion (bit spreading). SHA-256's internal compression function is essentially a block cipher operating on the message block; the hash output is the cipher's output. This is also why hash functions are closely related to PRFs: a collision-resistant hash function behaves like a pseudorandom function — indistinguishable from a truly random function given only its outputs.

🔑 Three Security Properties (Strongest to Weakest)
Collision resistance — it is infeasible to find any two distinct inputs m ≠ m' with H(m) = H(m'). The strongest property; implies the two below.

Second pre-image resistance — given a specific message m and its hash, it is infeasible to find a different m' such that H(m') = H(m). Protects existing signed documents from substitution.

Pre-image resistance — given only a hash value h, it is computationally infeasible to find any m with H(m) = h. The one-way property; the weakest of the three.

The Random Oracle Model

In security proofs, hash functions are often modelled as a random oracle — an ideal function that maps each input to a uniformly random output, with the constraint that the same input always gives the same output. No efficient algorithm can distinguish a random oracle from a truly random function. Real-world hash functions like SHA-256 are not provably random oracles, but they are designed to behave like one in practice. Many important security proofs (RSA-OAEP, ECDSA, HMAC security) rely on the random oracle assumption.

The Merkle-Damgård Construction

Most practical hash functions (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256) use the Merkle-Damgård construction: the message is padded to a multiple of the block size, split into fixed-size blocks, and processed iteratively through a compression function f with a running internal state:

// Merkle-Damgård processing chain IV → f(IV, block₁) → state₁ → f(state₁, block₂) → state₂ → ... → digest // SHA-256 specifics Block size: 512 bits (64 bytes) State size: 256 bits (8 × 32-bit words) Padding: append 1-bit, then zeros, then 64-bit message length Rounds: 64 compression rounds per block Output: 256-bit digest (last state value)

SHA-3 (Keccak) uses the sponge construction instead: it absorbs input blocks into a large internal state (1600 bits), then squeezes out the digest. The large state and absorption/squeezing design makes SHA-3 immune to length-extension attacks by design.

The Birthday Attack

By the birthday paradox, finding a collision in an n-bit hash requires only ~2n/2 evaluations — not 2n. This is the birthday bound: in a room of 23 people, there is a >50% chance of a shared birthday despite 365 possible birthdays — because the number of pairs grows as n²/2. The Seminar 4 portfolio exercises walk through this calculation explicitly.

MAC Security — UF-CMA and SUF-CMA

A MAC's security is defined in terms of a chosen-message attack (CMA) game: an attacker can request tags for any messages of their choice, then tries to forge a valid tag on a new message the server has not yet seen.

🔑 Two MAC Security Definitions (from Lecture 4)
UF-CMA (Unforgeability under Chosen-Message Attack) — the adversary cannot forge a valid tag on any new message they have not previously queried. They may have seen (message, tag) pairs for other messages, but cannot produce a valid tag for an un-queried one.

SUF-CMA (Strong Unforgeability under CMA) — strictly stronger: the adversary cannot produce any new valid (message, tag) pair, even if the message itself was previously queried. This prevents tag malleability — generating an alternate valid tag for an already-authenticated message.

Note: SUF-CMA ⟹ UF-CMA (every SUF-CMA secure MAC is also UF-CMA secure, but not vice versa). HMAC achieves SUF-CMA security. CBC-MAC achieves SUF-CMA only for fixed-length messages.

CBC-MAC

Before HMAC, the standard MAC construction was CBC-MAC: run the message through AES in CBC mode (with a zero IV) and use the final ciphertext block as the tag. The CBC chaining means any change to a plaintext block propagates through all subsequent blocks — Eve cannot alter any block without Bob detecting it.

// CBC-MAC computation state₀ = 0 (zero IV) state₁ = AES_K(state₀ ⊕ m₁) state₂ = AES_K(state₁ ⊕ m₂) ... tag = stateₙ (final block) // Security caveat (Lecture 4) CBC-MAC is SUF-CMA secure for FIXED-LENGTH messages only. For variable-length messages, it is NOT even UF-CMA secure — an attacker can construct forgeries by exploiting the length freedom.

NMAC and HMAC

The length-extension vulnerability of H(K ‖ m) motivates two safer constructions:

// NMAC (Nested MAC) — uses two independent keys k₁, k₂ NMAC(k₁, k₂, m) = H(k₂ ‖ H(k₁ ‖ m)) // HMAC — derives two keys from one using ipad/opad constants HMAC(K, m) = H((K ⊕ opad) ‖ H((K ⊕ ipad) ‖ m)) // ipad = 0x36 repeated; opad = 0x5C repeated // The outer hash takes K as part of its input → state is unreachable by attacker

Both NMAC and HMAC are SUF-CMA secure. The outer hash completely re-processes the key, so an attacker holding H(K ‖ m) cannot extend it — they cannot reach the outer hash's initial state without knowing K. HMAC is the practical choice: it requires only one key, is standardised in RFC 2104, and is directly supported by the Web Crypto API ('crypto.subtle.sign('HMAC', ...)').

Length-Extension Attacks

Merkle-Damgård hashes are vulnerable to length-extension attacks: given H(K ‖ m), an attacker can compute H(K ‖ m ‖ padding ‖ m') without knowing K. The attack works by resuming the Merkle-Damgård state machine from the digest value — which fully encodes the internal state after processing K ‖ m. SHA-3's sponge construction is immune because the full 1600-bit state is never revealed in the output.

IND-CCA Security via Authenticated Encryption

IND-CCA (Indistinguishability under Chosen Ciphertext Attack) is the gold standard: an adversary given access to a decryption oracle still cannot distinguish challenge ciphertexts. Achieving IND-CCA requires combining encryption with a MAC — specifically the Encrypt-then-MAC (EtM) pattern. AES-GCM achieves IND-CCA as an AEAD scheme (EtM with GHASH as the MAC).

Public Key Cryptography I — RSA

Public-key cryptography solved the fundamental key distribution problem: two parties can communicate securely without ever having shared a secret in advance. The insight is a trapdoor function — easy in one direction, hard to reverse without secret information.

Arithmetic Modulo n — The Mathematical Foundation

RSA is built on modular arithmetic. The key operation is modular exponentiation: x^e mod n. Two facts make this work:

// Fast computation: exponentiation by squaring x^e mod n can be computed in O(log e) multiplications // Invertibility: multiplicative inverses mod φ(n) If gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1, then there exists d such that e·d ≡ 1 mod φ(n) d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n), computed efficiently by the extended Euclidean algorithm // The RSA trapdoor: Euler's theorem For any x coprime to n: x^(φ(n)) ≡ 1 mod n Therefore: (x^e)^d ≡ x^(e·d) ≡ x^1 ≡ x mod n ✓

The Seminar 5 and 6 Python notebooks implement this arithmetic directly — computing modular inverses, verifying Euler's theorem, and running textbook RSA by hand on small numbers before scaling to the full 2048-bit case.

Quantifying Security: Security Parameter, Polynomial Time, and Negligible Advantage

Lecture 5 formalises what "secure" means precisely — this is CYBOK Week 5 Section 10.2.2, which the lecture explicitly covers:

🔑 Three Formal Security Concepts (Lecture 5)
Security parameter λ — the key length in bits, used to parameterise all security definitions. An encryption scheme has n-bit security if the best known attack requires 2ⁿ operations. Note: the security level n is not the same as the key length λ (e.g. RSA-2048 has ~112-bit security, not 2048-bit).

Polynomial time — an algorithm runs in polynomial time (i.e. is efficient) if its running time is bounded by a polynomial in the input length. Brute-force search is exponential time — this is why longer keys are secure. Security definitions require that no polynomial-time attacker can break the scheme.

Negligible advantage — a function f(λ) is negligible if it vanishes faster than any polynomial: for every polynomial p, limλ→∞ p(λ)·f(λ) = 0. An attacker's advantage in breaking a scheme must be negligible — even a tiny but non-negligible advantage would, given enough repetitions, allow reliable forgery or decryption.

Hardness Assumptions

Public-key security reduces to the assumed hardness of specific computational problems:

  • Integer Factorisation Problem (IFP) — given n = p × q (two large primes), find p and q. No polynomial-time classical algorithm is known; the best classical algorithm (GNFS) is sub-exponential. RSA security rests on this.
  • Discrete Logarithm Problem (DLP) — given g, p, and g^x mod p, find x. Underlies Diffie–Hellman and ElGamal.
  • Elliptic Curve DLP (ECDLP) — the DLP on elliptic curve groups; believed harder per bit than integer DLP, enabling smaller keys.

RSA Key Generation

// RSA key generation 1. Choose two large primes p and q (each ≥ 1024 bits; 2048-bit total modulus) 2. n = p × q (the modulus — public) 3. φ(n) = (p-1)(q-1) (Euler's totient — kept secret, destroyed after step 5) 4. e = 65537 (public exponent — standard choice, coprime to φ(n)) 5. d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n) (private exponent — computed via extended Euclidean algorithm) Public key: (e, n) // shared with everyone Private key: (d, n) // p, q, φ(n) MUST be securely deleted

Why e = 65537? It equals 2¹⁶ + 1 in binary (only two 1-bits), making encryption fast (16 squarings, 1 multiplication). It is large enough to avoid small-exponent attacks that affect e = 3.

RSA Encryption Standards — PKCS#1

Textbook RSA (c = m^e mod n) is deterministic and insecure. The PKCS#1 standard defines two secure padding schemes:

⚠️ RSA-PKCS#1 v1.5 vs RSA-OAEP Encryption
RSA-PKCS#1 v1.5 — adds a deterministic padding prefix before encrypting. Broken by the Bleichenbacher attack (1998): by submitting crafted ciphertexts to a server that reveals whether PKCS#1 padding is valid, an attacker can decrypt any ciphertext with ~1 million queries. Variants of this attack still affect real deployments today (ROBOT attack, 2018).

RSA-OAEP (Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding) — uses two hash functions and random salt to produce a randomised encoding. Proved IND-CCA secure under the RSA assumption (random oracle model). Standard in PKCS#1 v2.1. Always prefer RSA-OAEP for new systems.

RSA-KEM — Hybrid Encryption

Since RSA can only encrypt short messages (limited by the modulus size), real systems use a KEM-DEM hybrid scheme. Lecture 5 covers RSA-KEM explicitly:

// RSA-KEM: Key Encapsulation Mechanism + Data Encryption Mechanism 1. Alice generates a random session key K (e.g. 256-bit AES key) 2. Alice encapsulates K: C_kem = K^e mod n (RSA encryption of the session key) 3. Alice encrypts the message with K: C_dem = AES-GCM(K, message) 4. Alice sends (C_kem, C_dem) 5. Bob decapsulates: K = C_kem^d mod n (RSA decryption recovers session key) 6. Bob decrypts: message = AES-GCM_decrypt(K, C_dem) 7. Bob discards K // session key used once → compartmentalisation

Advantages of KEM-DEM: public-key crypto is used only for the short key (fast); symmetric crypto handles the bulk data (efficient); the session key is used once (compromise of one session doesn't affect others — compartmentalisation); the private key can be reused. Combined with AES-GCM, the whole system is IND-CCA secure via the composition theorem.

Digital Signatures — Syntax and Security

A digital signature provides authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation. Unlike a MAC (which requires both parties to share a secret key and therefore cannot provide non-repudiation), a signature uses an asymmetric key pair: anyone can verify using the public key, but only the holder of the private key can produce a valid signature.

🔑 Digital Signature Syntax (Three Algorithms)
KeyGen() → (v, s) — generates a public verification key v and private signing key s
Sign(s, m) → σ — produces a signature σ on message m using private key s
Verify(v, m, σ) → {0, 1} — checks whether σ is a valid signature on m under public key v

Security definition: SUF-CMA (Strong Unforgeability under Chosen-Message Attack) — an adversary who can request signatures on any messages of their choice cannot produce any new (message, signature) pair. This provides authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation.

Warning (DSKS attack): SUF-CMA security does not prevent a Duplicate Signature Key Selection (DSKS) attack: an attacker can craft an alternative key pair (v', s') such that (v', m, σ) also verifies — i.e. the same signature appears valid under two different public keys. This is relevant when a signature must be bound to a specific key identity (e.g. in certificate issuance).

RSA Signature Standards

// RSA-FDH (Full Domain Hash) — conceptually clean Sign: σ = H(m)^d mod n // hash must map onto the full Z*_n (impractical) Verify: σ^e ≡ H(m) mod n? // RSA-PKCS1-1.5 (legacy — no known practical attack on signatures, but no proof) Sign: σ = (0x01 || 0xFF...FF || 0x00 || H(m))^d mod n // deterministic padding before signing // RSA-PSS (modern standard — PKCS#1 v2.1) Sign: applies randomised salt before hashing → each signature is unique σ = PSS_encode(H(m), salt)^d mod n Verify: σ^e → PSS_decode → verify H(m) matches // RSA-PSS is provably secure (random oracle model). Use this for all new systems.

The Bleichenbacher attack on PKCS#1 v1.5 applies to encryption, not signatures — there is no known practical attack on RSA-PKCS1-1.5 signatures with strong hash functions. However, since there is no security proof, RSA-PSS (PKCS#1 v2.1) is preferred.

RSA Key Sizes and Security Levels

RSA security grows much more slowly than key length due to the GNFS sub-exponential factoring algorithm:

// RSA security levels (classical) RSA-1024: ~80-bit security ← legacy, NOT recommended (Seminar 5 default for illustration) RSA-2048: ~112-bit security ← current NIST minimum RSA-3072: ~128-bit security ← recommended for new deployments RSA-7680: ~192-bit security ← long-term (>2030) // Compare ECC (ECDLP has no known sub-exponential algorithm) ECC-256: ~128-bit security ← P-256, secp256k1 — 8× smaller key than RSA-3072 ECC-384: ~192-bit security ← P-384

Shor's algorithm on a sufficiently large quantum computer solves integer factorisation in polynomial time O((log N)³), breaking all RSA key sizes. NIST's post-quantum standards (ML-KEM, ML-DSA — published August 2024) are designed to replace RSA before large-scale quantum computers arrive.

🔐 Security Models (Modules 0–1)
Four assurances: Confidentiality · Integrity · Authentication · Non-repudiation
OW-PASS: weakest security goal — ciphertext must not reveal plaintext
IND-CPA: adversary cannot distinguish encryptions of chosen plaintexts
IND-CCA: strongest goal — holds even against a decryption oracle
Kerckhoffs's principle: security rests on key secrecy, never algorithm secrecy
🌊 Symmetric Cryptography (Modules 2–3)
One-time pad: perfect secrecy, impractical key length
Stream ciphers: PRG produces keystream from short key; nonce reuse is catastrophic
PRG / PRF / PRP: pseudorandom generator, function, permutation — security hierarchy
Block ciphers: DES (broken, 56-bit key), AES (standard, 128/192/256-bit)
Modes: ECB (insecure — ECB penguin) · CBC (IV required) · CTR (parallelisable)
AES-GCM: authenticated encryption — confidentiality + integrity in one
#️⃣ Hash Functions & MACs (Module 4)
Properties: pre-image resistance · second pre-image resistance · collision resistance
Birthday attack: finds collision in O(2^(n/2)) for n-bit hash — SHA-1 broken, SHA-256 secure
Merkle-Damgård: construction behind SHA-256; vulnerable to length-extension
HMAC: keyed MAC secure against length-extension; provides authentication
IND-CCA: achieved by combining cipher with MAC (Encrypt-then-MAC)
🔓 Public Key Cryptography (Module 5)
Trapdoor functions: easy to compute, hard to reverse without secret
RSA: based on integer factorisation; KeyGen selects primes p, q; encrypt with e, decrypt with d
RSA-OAEP: secure padding for encryption (PKCS#1v1.5 is legacy/broken for some uses)
Key insight: asymmetric crypto is slow — use it to establish shared keys, then switch to symmetric

Common Exam-Style Connections

  • Why does CBC require a random IV but CTR requires a unique nonce? Both ensure IND-CPA, but through different mechanisms.
  • Why can a plain hash H(K ‖ m) not be used as a MAC? Length-extension attacks allow forgery without K.
  • Why is RSA-2048 equivalent to only ~112 bits of security, not 2048 bits? The best factoring algorithms (NFS) run in sub-exponential time.
  • Why does AES-GCM require a fresh nonce per encryption? Nonce reuse leaks the authentication key, breaking both confidentiality and integrity.

Public Key Cryptography II — DHKE, ElGamal & ECC

This module extends public-key cryptography beyond RSA, covering the discrete-logarithm family — DHKE, ElGamal — and the significant efficiency gains from Elliptic Curve Cryptography. Seminar 6 implements RSA and ECC key generation with OpenSSL and explores the mathematics of public-key cryptography in Python.

Diffie–Hellman Key Exchange (DHKE)

DHKE (Diffie & Hellman, 1976) was the first published public-key protocol. It allows two parties to agree on a shared secret over a public channel with no prior communication. Security relies on the Computational Diffie–Hellman (CDH) problem: given g^a mod p and g^b mod p, compute g^(ab) mod p — believed hard for large primes p.

// DHKE — public parameters: prime p, generator g Alice: picks secret a, sends A = g^a mod p (public) Bob: picks secret b, sends B = g^b mod p (public) Alice: K = B^a mod p = g^(ab) mod p Bob: K = A^b mod p = g^(ab) mod p // Shared K — passive observer sees only g^a and g^b; CDH says K is hidden

Plain DHKE has no authentication — a man-in-the-middle can substitute their own public values (MitM attack). The Station-to-Station (STS) protocol fixes this with digital signatures (covered in Module 11).

ElGamal Encryption — DHKE Turned Into Encryption

ElGamal (1985) converts the DHKE idea into a full public-key encryption scheme. Unlike RSA, security rests on the Decisional Diffie–Hellman (DDH) problem rather than integer factorisation, and ElGamal ciphertexts are inherently randomised (semantically secure) without needing padding schemes like OAEP.

🔑 ElGamal — Full Protocol
Key generation: Bob picks private key b, computes public key B = g^b mod p. Public parameters (p, g, B); private key b is secret.

Encryption (Alice → Bob):
1. Alice picks a fresh random ephemeral key r (new r per message!)
2. Alice computes C₁ = g^r mod p (the ephemeral public component)
3. Alice computes C₂ = m · B^r mod p (message blinded by shared secret)
4. Alice sends ciphertext (C₁, C₂) = (g^r, m · B^r)

Decryption (Bob):
5. Bob computes the shared secret: s = C₁^b mod p = g^(rb) mod p
6. Bob recovers message: m = C₂ · s^(−1) mod p = m · B^r · (g^(rb))^(−1) = m ✓

Security: Semantic security under DDH — if an attacker can distinguish C₂ from random, they can solve DDH. The fresh r per message ensures the same plaintext produces different ciphertexts every time (IND-CPA).
// ElGamal worked example (small numbers for illustration) Public parameters: p = 23, g = 5 Bob's private key: b = 6 Bob's public key: B = g^b mod p = 5^6 mod 23 = 8 Alice encrypts m = 10 with ephemeral r = 3: C₁ = 5^3 mod 23 = 125 mod 23 = 10 C₂ = 10 · 8^3 mod 23 = 10 · 512 mod 23 = 10 · 6 = 60 mod 23 = 14 Ciphertext: (C₁, C₂) = (10, 14) Bob decrypts: s = C₁^b mod p = 10^6 mod 23 = 1000000 mod 23 = 6 m = C₂ · s^(−1) mod 23 = 14 · 6^(−1) mod 23 6^(−1) mod 23 = 4 (since 6·4 = 24 ≡ 1 mod 23) m = 14 · 4 mod 23 = 56 mod 23 = 10 ✓

Relationship to threshold cryptography: ElGamal's structure supports threshold decryption naturally (multiple parties each hold a share of b; they cooperate to compute s = g^(rb) without any party knowing b entirely). This is why ElGamal appears in distributed key generation and many advanced protocol constructions.

Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC)

An elliptic curve over a finite field is the set of points (x, y) satisfying y² = x³ + ax + b mod p plus a "point at infinity". Points form an abelian group under a geometric addition law:

// ECC point addition (geometric intuition) P + Q = R (draw a line through P and Q, reflect x-axis intersection) P + P = 2P (tangent to the curve at P, reflect intersection) Scalar multiplication: k·P = P + P + ... + P (k times, done efficiently via double-and-add)
🔑 Why ECC Gives Smaller Keys — The Security Level Table
The Elliptic Curve Discrete Log Problem (ECDLP) — given P and Q=kP on a curve, find k — has no known sub-exponential classical algorithm (unlike integer factorisation). This gives much better security per bit:

128-bit security: RSA-3072 (3072-bit key) ≈ ECC-256 (256-bit key) — 12× smaller key
192-bit security: RSA-7680 (7680-bit key) ≈ ECC-384 (384-bit key) — 20× smaller key
256-bit security: RSA-15360 (15360-bit key) ≈ ECC-521 (521-bit key) — 29× smaller key

Smaller keys mean: faster key generation, faster signing/verification, shorter TLS handshakes, smaller certificates, lower memory footprint — ideal for mobile, IoT, and high-throughput services.

ECDH and ECDSA

ECDH: replaces DHKE modular exponentiation with ECC scalar multiplication. Used in TLS 1.3 as ECDHE (ephemeral) for forward-secret key exchange. ECDSA: EC version of DSA; requires a fresh random nonce per signature (catastrophic if reused — see Developments module). Used in TLS certificates and Bitcoin transaction signing.

Standard Curves

P-256 (secp256r1) — NIST standard, used in TLS and FIDO2. secp256k1 — Bitcoin and Ethereum transactions. Curve25519 — designed by Bernstein with explicit side-channel resistance and transparent parameter choices; used in Signal, WireGuard, SSH, and WhatsApp.

Key Management

A cryptographic scheme is only as secure as its key management. Even a perfect algorithm fails if keys are generated weakly, stored insecurely, transported carelessly, or never revoked after compromise. This module covers the full Lecture 7 content: key life-cycle, key derivation, key formats (PEM), key distribution protocols (Kerberos), secret sharing (Shamir), and Public Key Infrastructure.

The Complete Key Life-Cycle

Lecture 7 identifies nine distinct stages — the app previously covered only seven. All nine matter for real deployments:

  1. Generation — keys are created from cryptographically secure random sources (CSPRNG). Weak randomness is catastrophic: Debian's flawed OpenSSL (2008) generated only ~32,000 distinct RSA keys across all Debian machines.
  2. Derivation — new keys are derived from an existing root key using a Key Derivation Function (KDF). Used when the root is too short (a password), not uniformly distributed (Diffie–Hellman output), or when you need multiple purpose-specific keys from one master secret.
  3. Transportation — moving keys to where they are needed. For symmetric keys: secure courier, hardware injection (SIMs, smart cards), or print-on-device. Public keys are simpler — only an authentic copy needs to reach the other party; the confidential private key never leaves the device.
  4. Storage — keys must be protected at rest. Options range from HSMs (tamper-resistant hardware, keys never extractable) to secure enclaves (ARM TrustZone, Intel SGX) to encrypted key vaults (HashiCorp Vault, AWS KMS).
  5. Usage — keys should be purpose-limited (a signing key should not encrypt; an encryption key should not sign). X.509 certificates encode permitted uses in the Key Usage extension.
  6. Update — keys are refreshed periodically or when required by policy. TLS session keys are ephemeral (discarded after each session for forward secrecy). Long-term certificate keys are typically rotated annually.
  7. Revocation — compromised keys must be invalidated before expiry. Mechanisms: Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs), OCSP, and Certificate Transparency logs.
  8. Archiving — keys may be retained long-term for auditing, legal discovery, or decryption of historical data. Archive keys require the same protection as active keys.
  9. Deletion — expired or superseded keys must be securely erased. Simple file deletion is insufficient — data must be overwritten or the storage medium destroyed.

Key Derivation Functions (KDFs)

KDFs produce cryptographic keys from a root input that may not itself be a uniformly random key:

🔑 Three Types of KDF
HKDF (HMAC-based KDF, RFC 5869) — two-stage: extract (compress non-uniform input to a pseudorandom key using HMAC) then expand (stretch to desired output length). Used in TLS 1.3 to derive traffic keys from the shared secret.

PBKDF2 (Password-Based KDF) — applies HMAC thousands of times (iteration count) to a password + salt. The high iteration count makes brute-force and pre-computation (rainbow tables) attacks expensive. Used for password storage and encrypted key files.

Argon2 — modern memory-hard KDF; winner of the Password Hashing Competition (2015). Configurable memory and time cost. Resistant to GPU and ASIC acceleration. Preferred for new password hashing deployments.

The PEM File Format (Privacy-Enhanced Mail)

PEM is the standard file format for storing and transmitting cryptographic objects. It encodes binary data (DER-encoded ASN.1 structures) as Base64, wrapped between header and footer lines. Base64 maps each group of 6 bits to one of 64 printable ASCII characters (2⁶ = 64).

// PEM format — the same Base64 wrapper for all types -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY----- // unencrypted private key (PKCS#8) MIIEvQIBADANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEF... // Base64-encoded DER data -----END PRIVATE KEY----- -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- // public key (SubjectPublicKeyInfo) MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOC... -----END PUBLIC KEY----- -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- // X.509 certificate MIIDazCCAlOgAwIBAgIUY3... -----END CERTIFICATE----- -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE REQUEST----- // CSR (Certificate Signing Request) MIICijCCAXICAQAwRTELMAk... -----END CERTIFICATE REQUEST-----

In the seminars, you used OpenSSL commands like openssl rsa -in key.pem -text -noout and openssl x509 -in cert.pem -text -noout to decode PEM files. The -text flag parses the Base64 and displays the human-readable structure; -noout suppresses the raw Base64 output.

Key Distribution — Kerberos

Distributing symmetric keys at scale is a fundamental problem: with N users communicating pairwise, you need N(N−1)/2 ≈ N² keys. Kerberos solves this by introducing a trusted third party — the Key Distribution Center (KDC). Each user shares only one secret key with the KDC. With N users, only N keys exist in total.

🎫 How Kerberos Works (Simplified)
1. Alice wants to talk to Bob. She sends a request to the KDC: "I am Alice; I want a session key for Bob."

2. The KDC generates a fresh session key K_AB and returns: (a) K_AB encrypted under Alice's long-term key K_A, and (b) a ticket — K_AB encrypted under Bob's long-term key K_B (the "ticket to Bob").

3. Alice decrypts her part to get K_AB. She forwards the ticket (which she cannot decrypt) to Bob.

4. Bob decrypts the ticket using K_B, recovers K_AB, and both parties now share the session key — without the KDC ever needing to transmit K_AB in cleartext.

Real-world use: Kerberos is the authentication backbone of Microsoft Active Directory. When you log into a Windows machine and automatically access file servers, printers, and internal applications without re-entering your password, that is Kerberos Single Sign-On (SSO) in action.

Shamir Secret Sharing (SSS)

Some keys are too valuable to store in a single location — a root CA private key, a cryptocurrency wallet master key, a nuclear launch authorisation code. Shamir Secret Sharing (Shamir, 1979) splits a secret K into n shares such that any t shares reconstruct K exactly, but any t−1 or fewer shares reveal nothing about K.

📐 How SSS Works — Polynomial Interpolation
To create a (t, n) threshold scheme for secret K:

1. Share generation: Choose a random polynomial f(x) of degree t−1 where f(0) = K. For example, for (2, 3): pick random a, set f(x) = K + ax. Give share 1 = f(1), share 2 = f(2), share 3 = f(3) to three custodians.

2. Reconstruction: Any 2 custodians can apply Lagrange interpolation to their two points and recover the unique line f(x), then evaluate f(0) = K.

3. Information-theoretic security: With only 1 share (one point on the line), all values of K are equally likely — the share reveals nothing. This is perfect secrecy, not just computational security.

Real-world examples: Root CA key ceremonies (e.g. DNSSEC root key is held by 7 custodians across 14 key ceremony participants), multi-party cryptocurrency wallet recovery, certificate authority master key protection.
// (2, 3) Shamir example over integers (simplified — real SSS uses a prime field) Secret K = 42, random coefficient a = 7 Polynomial: f(x) = 42 + 7x Share 1: f(1) = 49 → Custodian A Share 2: f(2) = 56 → Custodian B Share 3: f(3) = 63 → Custodian C Reconstruction with shares 1 and 2 (Lagrange interpolation): f(0) = 49 · (0−2)/(1−2) + 56 · (0−1)/(2−1) = 49 · 2 + 56 · (−1) = 98 − 56 = 42 ✓

Public Key Infrastructure (PKI)

PKI binds public keys to verified identities via digitally signed X.509 certificates. Every certificate contains: subject identity (distinguished name), public key, issuer (CA) identity, validity period, permitted key usages, and the CA's digital signature over all the above.

🔑 Certificate Validation — What Your Browser Actually Checks
When your browser connects to a website over HTTPS, it performs all of these checks:

1. Chain verification — the server certificate is signed by an intermediate CA, which is signed by a root CA in the browser's trust store. Every signature in the chain must verify.
2. Subject matching — the certificate's Subject Alternative Names (SANs) must include the domain you requested.
3. Validity period — the current time must be within notBefore and notAfter.
4. Revocation check — via OCSP (real-time) or CRL (periodic list). If revoked, connection is rejected.
5. Certificate Transparency — modern browsers require that certificates are logged in public CT logs before they are trusted. This allows anyone to audit all issued certificates and detect misissuance.

Certificate Transparency (CT)

CT (Google, 2013; now RFC 6962) adds public, append-only logs that record every certificate issued by every CA. When a CA issues a certificate, it must submit it to at least two CT logs; the logs return a Signed Certificate Timestamp (SCT) that is embedded in the certificate. Browsers refuse certificates without valid SCTs.

CT solved a real problem: in 2011, the Dutch CA DigiNotar was compromised and issued fraudulent certificates for Google, Mozilla, and CIA domains — attackers used these for MitM attacks on Iranian citizens. With CT, such misissuance would be publicly visible within hours and the fraudulent certificates could be blocked before they caused harm.

Threats to PKI Security

PKI security rests on a chain of trust — and every link in the chain is a potential failure point:

  • CA compromise — if a CA's private signing key is stolen, every certificate it has issued becomes untrustworthy. The entire CA must be shut down and all its certificates revoked (as happened with DigiNotar and Comodo 2011).
  • Fraudulent issuance — a CA issuing certificates for domains it has not properly verified. CT logs exist specifically to detect this.
  • Revocation failures — users who cannot access OCSP or CRL endpoints may unknowingly trust revoked certificates. "Soft-fail" OCSP is a common browser default — if the OCSP server is unreachable, the certificate is treated as valid.
  • Key compromise — stealing the private key of any certificate in the chain enables impersonation until revocation.

Protocols I — Authentication Protocols

A cryptographic protocol is a precisely specified multi-step message exchange that achieves a security goal — authentication, key establishment, or privacy — between parties who may not fully trust each other or the channel. Lecture 8 covers three authentication protocol families, then shows how real-world systems (Kerberos, PGP) deploy them.

Three Approaches to Entity Authentication

Protocols prove identity in three structurally different ways, each with distinct security properties:

🔑 Authentication Protocol Families (Lecture 8)
1. MAC-based — prover demonstrates knowledge of a shared symmetric key K by computing MAC(K, nonce); the verifier recomputes and compares. Provides authentication but not non-repudiation (both parties know K). Example: Kerberos ticket authentication.

2. Encryption-based — verifier encrypts a random challenge under the claimant's public key; only the genuine claimant can decrypt and return it. Provides authentication and non-repudiation. Example: TLS client certificate challenge.

3. Zero-knowledge-based — prover convinces verifier of a secret without revealing any information about the secret itself. Provides authentication without ever transmitting the secret. Example: Schnorr identification, zk-SNARKs.

Challenge–Response Authentication

The most common authentication pattern: the verifier issues a fresh nonce (number used once); the prover responds with a value that could only be produced by the holder of the secret. Freshness prevents replay attacks.

// MAC-based challenge–response Verifier → Prover: nonce r (fresh random value) Prover → Verifier: MAC(K, r) // only K-holder can produce this Verifier: recompute MAC(K, r) and compare // Encryption-based challenge–response (signature variant from Lecture 8) Verifier → Prover: nonce N (fresh random challenge) Prover → Verifier: σ = Sign(sk_prover, N) // proves private key possession Verifier: Verify(pk_prover, N, σ) → accept/reject

Man-in-the-Middle Attacks on Authentication Protocols

Without proper authentication, an attacker can impersonate either party or relay messages to trick both sides. Lecture 8 emphasises three MitM capabilities:

  • Impersonate the prover to the verifier — claim to be Alice when talking to Bob
  • Impersonate the verifier to the prover — claim to be Bob when talking to Alice
  • Relay or modify messages — pass messages between Alice and Bob while reading or altering them

Secure authentication protocols defeat all three by binding each message to a fresh nonce and a verified identity.

Kerberos — MAC-Based Authentication in Practice

Kerberos is covered in both Lecture 7 (key management) and Lecture 8 (authentication protocols), because it illustrates both concerns. In Lecture 8's framing, Kerberos is a MAC-based authentication protocol that uses symmetric encryption to prove identity without transmitting passwords over the network.

🎫 Kerberos as an Authentication Protocol
Setup: Each principal (Alice, Bob, services) shares a long-term symmetric key with the KDC. These are derived from passwords via a KDF — the password never travels over the network.

Authentication exchange:
1. Alice → KDC: "I am Alice; give me access to Bob's service."
2. KDC → Alice: {session key K_AB}_{K_Alice} plus a ticket {K_AB, Alice's identity}_{K_Bob}
3. Alice decrypts her part; forwards the ticket to Bob
4. Alice → Bob: ticket + authenticator = {timestamp}_{K_AB}
5. Bob decrypts ticket (recovers K_AB), decrypts authenticator, verifies timestamp is fresh

What makes this secure: The authenticator is a MAC over a fresh timestamp — Bob verifies it was just produced. Replaying it later fails because the timestamp would be stale. The ticket is opaque to Alice — she forwards it without being able to modify it.

Real-world deployment: Microsoft Active Directory uses Kerberos v5 for all domain authentication. Every Windows SSO login (opening shared drives, printers, internal apps without re-entering credentials) uses this protocol.

PGP — Authority-Free Encryption and Signing

PGP (Pretty Good Privacy, Phil Zimmermann, 1991) — and its open standard successor OpenPGP (RFC 4880) — is an encryption and digital signature system for email and files that operates without a Certificate Authority. This distinguishes it fundamentally from the Web PKI.

🔑 PGP's Web of Trust vs. PKI's Hierarchy
Web PKI (CAs): trust flows top-down from pre-installed root CAs. You trust a certificate because the CA vouches for it. Centralised, efficient, but relies on CA integrity.

PGP Web of Trust: trust is peer-to-peer. Alice trusts Bob's key if she has met Bob in person and signed his key, or if Charlie (whom Alice already trusts) has signed Bob's key. Trust propagates through a social network of key signatures — no central authority needed.

PGP encryption flow:
1. Alice fetches Bob's public key (from a key server or directly)
2. Alice generates a random session key K
3. Alice encrypts the message with K using AES
4. Alice encrypts K with Bob's RSA public key
5. Alice sends both (this is PGP's KEM-DEM hybrid encryption)
6. Alice optionally signs the message with her RSA/DSA private key

Limitation: The web of trust requires users to manage their own key verification — a burden most users find impractical. PGP adoption has been limited by this usability problem. Modern alternatives (Signal, Wire) use different trust models with automatic key verification.

Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKP)

A ZKP allows a prover to convince a verifier they know a secret without revealing any information about the secret. Three properties must hold simultaneously:

  • Completeness — an honest prover who knows the secret always convinces the verifier
  • Soundness — a cheating prover who does not know the secret cannot convince the verifier (except with negligible probability)
  • Zero-knowledge — the verifier learns nothing beyond the truth of the statement — not even a single bit of the secret
📌 ZKP in Practice — Schnorr Identification (Seminar 9)
The Schnorr protocol (Seminar 9 exercises) proves knowledge of a discrete log x (where y = g^x mod p) without revealing x. Three phases:

Commit: Peggy picks random r, sends t = g^r mod p
Challenge: Victor sends random c
Respond: Peggy sends s = (r + c·x) mod (p−1)
Verify: Victor checks g^s ≡ t · y^c mod p

Why zero-knowledge? A simulator can generate indistinguishable transcripts without knowing x: pick random s and c, compute t = g^s · y^(−c) mod p. This transcript (t, c, s) passes verification but x was never used. Schnorr's protocol is the foundation of ECDSA and the Fiat–Shamir transform (used to convert interactive proofs into digital signatures).

Applications of ZKPs

Password authentication — prove password knowledge without transmitting the password (used in PAKE protocols). Anonymous credentials — prove membership of a group without revealing identity. zk-SNARKs — succinct non-interactive ZKPs used in Zcash and Ethereum L2 rollups for privacy-preserving computations at scale. Blockchain privacy — Lecture 9 explicitly notes that ZKPs let users prove they have sufficient funds without revealing amounts or addresses.

Protocols I — Authentication

A protocol is a multi-step exchange of messages between parties that achieves a shared security goal. This module focuses on entity authentication — proving identity without revealing secrets.

Challenge–Response Authentication

The most common pattern: the verifier sends a random challenge; the prover responds with a value that proves knowledge of a secret (e.g. an HMAC or signature over the challenge). A fresh challenge prevents replay attacks.

// Challenge–response with MAC Verifier → Prover: nonce r Prover → Verifier: MAC(K, r) // only holder of K can produce this Verifier: recompute MAC(K, r) and compare

Encryption-Based Authentication

Authentication can also be based on asymmetric encryption: the verifier encrypts a random value under the claimant's public key; only the genuine claimant can decrypt and return it.

Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKP)

🔑 Zero-Knowledge Proofs
A ZKP allows a prover to convince a verifier that they know a secret without revealing the secret itself. Three properties: Completeness (honest prover always convinces), Soundness (cheating prover fails), Zero-knowledge (verifier learns nothing beyond the truth of the statement).

Key Establishment & TLS

Key establishment protocols allow two parties to agree on session keys for subsequent symmetric encryption. There are two fundamentally different approaches, with very different security properties.

Key Transport vs. Key Agreement

🔑 Two Approaches to Establishing a Shared Key
Key transport — one party generates the session key and encrypts it under the other party's public key (e.g. RSA-encrypted pre-master secret in TLS 1.2). Simple, but lacks forward secrecy: compromise of the long-term private key later decrypts all past sessions.

Key agreement — both parties contribute randomness; neither party can control the resulting key (e.g. Diffie–Hellman). With ephemeral keys, provides forward secrecy: past session keys cannot be recovered even if long-term keys are later compromised. TLS 1.3 mandates key agreement only.

Plain DHKE — Worked Numerical Example (Seminar 10)

Seminar 10 uses these exact parameters. Working through the arithmetic by hand is the most direct way to understand DHKE:

// Seminar 10 DHKE parameters Public parameters: p = 23 (prime), g = 5 (generator) Alice's private key: a = 6 Bob's private key: b = 15 // Step 1: Each party computes their public value Alice's public key: A = g^a mod p = 5^6 mod 23 5^1 = 5, 5^2 = 25 ≡ 2, 5^3 = 10, 5^4 = 50 ≡ 4, 5^5 = 20, 5^6 = 100 ≡ 8 mod 23 A = 8 Bob's public key: B = g^b mod p = 5^15 mod 23 5^6 = 8 (from above), 5^12 = 8^2 = 64 ≡ 18, 5^15 = 5^12 · 5^3 = 18 · 10 = 180 ≡ 180 − 7·23 = 19 B = 19 // Step 2: Each party computes the shared secret Alice computes: K = B^a mod p = 19^6 mod 23 19 ≡ −4 mod 23, (−4)^2 = 16, (−4)^3 = −64 ≡ −64 + 3·23 = 5 (−4)^6 = ((−4)^3)^2 = 5^2 = 25 ≡ 2 mod 23 K = 2 Bob computes: K = A^b mod p = 8^15 mod 23 8^2 = 64 ≡ 18, 8^4 = 18^2 = 324 ≡ 324 − 14·23 = 2 8^8 = 2^2 = 4, 8^15 = 8^8 · 8^4 · 8^2 · 8^1 = 4 · 2 · 18 · 8 = 1152 1152 mod 23: 1152 / 23 = 50.08..., 50 × 23 = 1150, 1152 − 1150 = 2 K = 2 ✓ (same shared secret!)

An observer sees only A = 8, B = 19, g = 5, p = 23. To find K = 2, they must solve the Discrete Logarithm Problem: find a such that 5^a ≡ 8 mod 23. For real DHKE, p has 2048+ bits — this is computationally infeasible.

MitM Attack With Eve — Seminar 10 Exercise

Seminar 10 also asks: what if Eve intercepts A and B, inserts her own public key E = g^e mod p with e = 10?

// Seminar 10 MitM calculation (e = 10) Eve's public key: E = 5^10 mod 23 5^10 = (5^5)^2 = 20^2 = 400 ≡ 400 − 17·23 = 9 E = 9 Alice-Eve shared secret: K_AE = E^a mod p = 9^6 mod 23 9^2 = 81 ≡ 81 − 3·23 = 12, 9^3 = 9·12 = 108 ≡ 108 − 4·23 = 16 9^6 = 16^2 = 256 ≡ 256 − 11·23 = 3 K_AE = 3 Bob-Eve shared secret: K_BE = E^b mod p = 9^15 mod 23 9^3 = 16 (from above), 9^6 = 3, 9^12 = 3^2 = 9, 9^15 = 9^12·9^3 = 9·16 = 144 ≡ 144 − 6·23 = 6 K_BE = 6 // Result: Alice and Bob have DIFFERENT shared secrets Alice thinks she shares K_AE = 3 with "Bob" (actually Eve) Bob thinks he shares K_BE = 6 with "Alice" (actually Eve) Eve knows both K_AE = 3 and K_BE = 6 — she can decrypt, re-encrypt, and relay all traffic

This is exactly why plain DHKE is insufficient: Alice and Bob cannot tell that the public values they received came from a legitimate party. The STS protocol below fixes this.

Authenticated DHKE

Adding authentication to DHKE requires binding the key exchange to verified identities. Two methods: (1) sign the DH public values with a long-term key; (2) use a pre-shared key to authenticate the exchange. TLS 1.3 uses certificate-based signatures over the transcript.

The Station-to-Station (STS) Protocol

STS (Diffie, van Oorschot, Wiener, 1992) is the canonical solution combining DHKE with mutual authentication and forward secrecy:

// STS Protocol — full authenticated key exchange 1. Alice → Bob: g^a mod p 2. Bob → Alice: g^b mod p, E_K(Sig_Bob(g^b, g^a)) 3. Alice → Bob: E_K(Sig_Alice(g^a, g^b)) // K = g^(ab) mod p — derived from the DH exchange // Signatures are ENCRYPTED under K — prevents identity stripping
📌 Four Security Properties of STS
1. Key agreement — shared session key K = g^(ab) is derived jointly; neither party unilaterally controls it
2. Mutual authentication — each party's signature over the DH values proves identity; forged values are detected
3. Forward secrecy — fresh ephemeral exponents a, b are discarded after the session; compromising long-term keys later reveals nothing about K
4. Key confirmation — encrypting the signature under K proves both parties derived the same K

The Unknown Key Share (UKS) Attack

A subtle but serious attack where two honest parties agree on a valid key, but each believes the key is shared with a different partner. Mallory does not learn K — but Alice thinks she's talking to Mallory, while Mallory convinces Bob the key is shared with Alice.

// UKS Attack — identities are confused, not the key Alice → Mallory: g^a (Alice believes she is talking to Mallory) Mallory → Bob: g^a (Mallory forwards, Bob believes he is talking to Alice) Bob → Mallory: g^b Mallory → Alice: g^b Result: K = g^(ab) is correct, but: - Alice thinks K is shared with Mallory - Bob thinks K is shared with Alice - Mallory can later attribute messages from Alice to herself with Bob

Countermeasure: include explicit identity labels inside the signed transcript (STS-MAC variant). TLS prevents UKS by including the server's certificate identity in the signed handshake transcript.

Real-World Key Establishment Protocols

🌐 TLS · IPSec · SSH
TLS 1.3 — mandates ECDHE (ephemeral) for key agreement; authenticates with certificate signatures over the full transcript; derives session keys via HKDF. No static RSA key exchange (removed for lack of forward secrecy).

IKEv2 / IPSec — uses DHKE or ECDHE for key agreement; authentication via certificates or pre-shared keys; operates at the IP layer securing VPN tunnels.

SSH — uses ECDH or DH for key agreement; server authenticated via host key (Trust On First Use for first connection; stored in known_hosts thereafter). Client authenticated via public key or password.

Password-Authenticated Key Exchange (PAKE)

PAKE (e.g. SRP, OPAQUE) is a special class combining key agreement with password authentication — without transmitting the password or a hash of it. Neither party can mount an offline dictionary attack from the transcript alone. Used in secure password managers and some enterprise VPN systems.

Attacks

Even theoretically secure algorithms can be broken in practice. This module covers the full attack taxonomy from Lecture 10: side-channel attacks, mathematical cryptanalysis, and integer factorisation — along with the key distinction between what is and is not a side-channel attack.

Attack Vectors — Two Fundamental Categories

⚔️ Algorithmic vs Side-Channel Attacks
Algorithmic / mathematical attacks — exploit mathematical structure in the algorithm itself. Target the cipher, hash, or protocol design. Require no physical access.

Side-channel attacks — exploit implementation or physical leakage: timing, power consumption, electromagnetic emissions, cache state. The algorithm may be perfectly correct; the vulnerability is in how it is executed.

What Is NOT a Side-Channel Attack

A common exam error — Lecture 10 explicitly clarifies these are not side-channel attacks:

// These exploit protocol/mathematical properties — not physical leakage Replay attacks → exploit protocol logic Cut-and-paste → exploit lack of integrity (no authentication) Frequency analysis → exploit statistical properties of plaintext Birthday attacks → exploit mathematical hash output space Brute-force search → exploit computational search space Man-in-the-middle → exploit message interception/routing Unknown Key Share → exploit protocol design flaw (UKS)

Side-Channel Attacks

  • Timing attacks — measure execution time variation to infer key bits. RSA decryption time varies depending on which bits of d are set (square-and-multiply). A non-constant-time string comparison leaks the prefix of the correct hash one byte at a time. Kocher (1996) demonstrated practical timing attacks against RSA implementations.
  • Power analysis (SPA / DPA) — measure device current draw during cryptographic operations. Simple Power Analysis (SPA) reads a single trace; Differential Power Analysis (DPA) statistically correlates many traces against hypothesised key byte values. The correlation reveals the actual key byte by byte.
  • Electromagnetic (EM) leakage — capture EM emissions from chips during computation. EM analysis can recover AES keys from contactless smart cards at distances of centimetres.
  • Cache-timing / Spectre — exploit CPU cache access patterns. Spectre (2018) showed that speculative execution in modern CPUs creates side channels between processes sharing a CPU, bypassing OS memory isolation.
🛡️ Countermeasures
Constant-time implementations — all code paths take the same time regardless of secret values (e.g. compare full HMAC tag before returning result, never early-exit)
Blinding / masking — multiply RSA input by a random value before exponentiation; unmask the result (the random factor cancels in the exponent but decorrelates timing from key bits)
Physical shielding — Faraday caging, power filtering, and physical tamper detection in HSMs
Noise injection — add random delays or dummy operations to obscure timing signals

Mathematical Cryptanalysis

Linear cryptanalysis (Matsui, 1993) — finds linear approximations of the S-boxes and uses them to build a statistical distinguisher. Given enough plaintext-ciphertext pairs, a bias in the XOR of selected bits reveals key information. Drove the AES S-box design (chosen for low linearity bias).

Differential cryptanalysis (Biham & Shamir, 1990) — studies how XOR differences in plaintext pairs propagate through cipher rounds. By choosing many pairs with a fixed input difference Δ, the output difference distribution is not uniform, revealing information about the last round key. AES MixColumns was specifically designed with high branch numbers to defeat this.

🔢 Integer Factorisation — Attacking RSA
Integer factorisation is distinct from linear/differential cryptanalysis: it targets asymmetric (public-key) systems, not symmetric ones.

Trial division — test all primes up to √n. Practical only for small n.
Fermat's method — exploits the fact that n = ((p+q)/2)² − ((p-q)/2)². Fast when p and q are close together — never use primes within 2^(n/4) of each other.
Pollard's rho algorithm — probabilistic, runs in O(n^(1/4)) — broke RSA-100 (330-bit) in 1991.
General Number Field Sieve (GNFS) — best classical algorithm, sub-exponential: L[1/3, 1.923]. Broke RSA-768 (2009) and RSA-829 (2020, largest factored to date). RSA-2048 requires ~10^(17) GNFS operations — currently infeasible classically.
Shor's algorithm — polynomial time O((log N)³) on a quantum computer. Breaks all RSA key sizes once large-scale quantum computers are available.

Provable Security and Formal Methods

Provable security formalises the connection between breaking a scheme and solving a known hard problem (e.g. factoring). A proof shows: if you can break RSA-OAEP, then you can solve the RSA problem. This does not mean the scheme is unconditionally secure — it means it is as hard as the underlying assumption. Formal methods (Tamarin, ProVerif) can verify protocol security properties mechanically, finding flaws that mathematical analysis misses.

Developments in Cryptography

This module covers the final frontier of the course: how digital signatures work and their security pitfalls, how signatures are extended with special properties for privacy and threshold control, the ongoing global transition to quantum-resistant algorithms, and how core cryptographic primitives underpin modern blockchain and cryptocurrency systems.

Part 1 — Digital Signatures

A digital signature provides authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation: the signer cannot later deny having signed. Every scheme has three algorithms:

  • KeyGen() → (pk, sk) — generates a signing key pair
  • Sign(sk, m) → σ — produces signature σ on message m
  • Verify(pk, m, σ) → {accept, reject} — checks validity

The Hash-and-Sign Paradigm

Signing a full message is expensive. The standard approach hashes first, then signs only the fixed-size digest: σ = Sign(sk, H(m)). Security depends on both the signature scheme and the hash function — a broken hash enables signature forgery via collision.

// Hash-and-sign: ECDSA with SHA-256 1. d = SHA-256(m) (32 bytes — fixed size) 2. k = fresh random nonce (CRITICAL: must be unique per signature) 3. r = (k·G).x mod n (point on elliptic curve) 4. s = k⁻¹(d + r·sk) mod n Signature σ = (r, s) Verify: check (s⁻¹·d·G + s⁻¹·r·pk).x ≡ r mod n
⚠️ ECDSA Nonce Reuse — Catastrophic Failure
If the same nonce k is used for two ECDSA signatures on different messages, the private key sk is fully recoverable: sk = (s₁·d₂ − s₂·d₁) / (s₁ − s₂) mod n.

Sony PS3 (2010): A static nonce broke the console's signing key — all software authentication was defeated.
Bitcoin wallet drains: Android's weak random number generator in early versions caused nonce collisions, emptying wallets.

Fix — EdDSA (Ed25519, Ed448): Derives the nonce deterministically from H(sk ‖ m). Cannot repeat for distinct messages. No entropy dependency. Preferred for all new designs.

RSA-PSS

RSA-PSS (Probabilistic Signature Scheme) is the modern RSA signature standard. A randomised salt is included in padding before signing, making each signature unique even for identical messages. RSA-PSS is provably secure in the random oracle model. Older RSA-PKCS#1v1.5 is deterministic and has known bleichenbacher-style vulnerabilities in some contexts.

Real-World Applications

Digital signatures underpin: TLS certificates (CA signs server public key), code signing (authenticates software binaries), blockchain transactions (ECDSA/secp256k1 in Bitcoin, Ed25519 in Solana), DNSSEC (authenticates DNS records), and e-government (document signing, passports).

Part 2 — Advanced Signature Schemes

Blind Signatures

A blind signature lets a signer authenticate a message without ever seeing its content. The protocol (Chaum, 1982) has four steps:

// Blind signature protocol (RSA-based) 1. User picks random blinding factor r, computes m' = m · r^e mod n 2. User sends blinded message m' to signer 3. Signer signs: σ' = (m')^d mod n (signer sees only m' — not m) 4. User unblinds: σ = σ' · r⁻¹ mod n // σ is a valid RSA signature on m — signer cannot link σ to their session
🔑 Blind Signature Security Properties
Message privacy — signer learns nothing about m from m'
Unforgeability — user cannot obtain signatures on messages they did not submit
Unlinkability — signer cannot match a produced signature σ back to the session in which m' was signed

Applications: DigiCash e-cash (bank signs coins without learning serial numbers · 1989), anonymous voting systems (authority signs ballot without knowing voter choice), privacy-preserving credential issuance (W3C Anonymous Credential specifications).

Ring Signatures

A ring signature proves a message was signed by exactly one member of a defined group — but makes it computationally infeasible to determine which member signed. The signer uses everyone's public keys to construct the signature; no group setup or coordinator is needed.

🔑 Ring Signature Properties & Applications
Signer ambiguity — verifier can confirm a group member signed but cannot identify who
Spontaneous — the signer can form the ring unilaterally from any set of public keys
Unforgeable — only actual group members can produce valid ring signatures

Applications: whistleblower document authentication (confirms source is within an organisation), Monero cryptocurrency (transaction senders are hidden among a ring of decoys), academic peer review anonymity systems.

Threshold Signatures

A (k, n) threshold signature scheme requires any k of n designated parties to cooperate to produce a valid signature. The private key is split via secret sharing — no individual ever holds the full key.

  • k-of-n Bitcoin multi-sig: a wallet controlled by 3 parties requires any 2 to authorise a transaction (2-of-3) — no single point of failure
  • Distributed Certificate Authorities: root CA key material split across geographically separated HSMs — no single CA server can be coerced into signing a malicious certificate alone
  • MPC wallets: institutional cryptocurrency custody uses multi-party computation to produce a signature without ever assembling the full key in one location

Part 3 — Post-Quantum Cryptography (NIST Standards 2024)

⚛️ The Quantum Threat — Two Algorithms
Shor's algorithm (1994, polynomial time) — solves integer factorisation (breaks RSA) and discrete logarithm (breaks DHKE, ECDSA, ElGamal, ECDH). All current asymmetric algorithms are broken by a sufficiently large quantum computer.

Grover's algorithm (quadratic speedup only) — halves the effective key length of symmetric ciphers and hash functions. AES-128 drops to 64-bit security (borderline); AES-256 retains ~128-bit security — still strong. Symmetric crypto needs key-length doubling at most. The urgent replacement problem is entirely asymmetric.
🔑 NIST PQC Standards — Published August 2024
NIST launched a public competition in 2016; 69 candidates submitted, whittled down over four rounds. Three standards published August 2024:

FIPS 203 — ML-KEM (CRYSTALS-Kyber) · Lattice-based KEM
  Replaces RSA/ECDH key exchange · Key sizes: 800–1568 bytes (vs 256 bytes for ECDH-256)

FIPS 204 — ML-DSA (CRYSTALS-Dilithium) · Lattice-based signatures
  Replaces RSA-PSS/ECDSA · Signature sizes: 2420–4627 bytes (vs 64 bytes for Ed25519)

FIPS 205 — SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) · Hash-based signatures
  Conservative fallback — security based only on hash function properties, not lattice hardness assumptions · Larger signatures (~8 KB), but relies on no new maths

All three resist Shor's algorithm. Integration work underway in IETF (TLS, SSH) and ETSI. Google and Cloudflare already experimenting with hybrid TLS deployments.

Hybrid Deployment Strategy

Because PQC schemes are new and may have undiscovered weaknesses, the recommended near-term strategy is hybrid mode: combine a classical algorithm (e.g. ECDH P-256) with a PQC algorithm (e.g. ML-KEM) in the same handshake. The session key is derived from both — if either algorithm holds, the session is secure. This provides a safety net while the community gains confidence in the new standards.

// Hybrid TLS key exchange (experimental, 2024) Session key = KDF(ECDH_shared_secret ‖ ML-KEM_shared_secret) // Classical attacker: must break ECDH (computationally infeasible today) // Quantum attacker: must break ML-KEM (lattice problem — believed hard) // Both attackers: must break BOTH simultaneously

Part 4 — Blockchain & Cryptocurrency

Blockchain systems are not a new type of cryptography — they are a carefully engineered composition of the primitives studied throughout this course. The innovation is architectural, not cryptographic.

🔗 Bitcoin — A Cryptographic Primitive Map
SHA-256 (hash functions) — two roles: (1) block chaining — each block header includes H(previous block header), making the chain tamper-evident; (2) proof-of-work — miners find a nonce n such that SHA-256(SHA-256(block header ‖ n)) has ≥ T leading zeros (difficulty target T adjusts every 2016 blocks)

Merkle trees (hash trees) — all transactions in a block are hashed pairwise up to a single 32-byte Merkle root stored in the header. A Merkle proof lets a lightweight node verify one transaction in O(log n) hashes without downloading all transactions

ECDSA secp256k1 (digital signatures) — every Bitcoin transaction is authorised by the sender's ECDSA signature over the transaction data; the network verifies against the sender's public key (which, when hashed, gives the Bitcoin address)

RIPEMD-160(SHA-256(pk)) (address derivation) — Bitcoin addresses are derived by hashing the public key twice, providing a compact, collision-resistant identifier

Zero-Knowledge Proofs in Blockchain

zk-SNARKs (Zero-Knowledge Succinct Non-Interactive Arguments of Knowledge) allow a prover to convince a verifier that a computation was performed correctly, without revealing any of the inputs. Three properties:

  • Zero-knowledge — verifier learns nothing about inputs beyond the output being correct
  • Succinct — proof is tiny (a few hundred bytes) regardless of computation size
  • Non-interactive — no back-and-forth; proof is a single message the verifier checks offline
// zk-SNARK use cases in cryptocurrency Zcash (shielded transactions): Prover: "I spent a valid coin and created a valid output" Verifier: checks the proof — confirms no double-spend, valid amounts Learns: nothing about sender, recipient, or amount Ethereum L2 rollups (zkEVM): Operator: executes 10,000 transactions off-chain Posts: one zk-SNARK proof to Ethereum mainnet Ethereum: verifies the proof (~200,000 gas vs ~2.1 billion gas for all txns individually) Result: ~10,000× throughput increase with full cryptographic security guarantees

zk-SNARKs are now also used outside blockchain: anonymous credentials (proving age without revealing date of birth), private set intersection (two parties find common elements without revealing their lists), and verifiable computation outsourcing.
